latin.2097: THESIS I. JACOBUS Arminius, & qui ejus dogmata in Belgio secuti Remonstrantes dicuntur, quemadmodum in explicanda libertatis humanae natura, cum Molina & ejus discipulis consentiunt; ita quoque videntur eam eodem modo cum Providentiae Divinae decretis conciliare. Saltem huc tendunt quae docet Arminius Responsione ad Articulum 7. Operum ipsius pagina 143. Ubi non negat quidem Deum Decreto suo aeterno futura contingentia praedefinivisse & praedeterminasse; sed distinguit duplicem Dei determinationem qua statuit ut aliquid fiat: Unam talem, qua, posita qualicunque actione, motione, impulsu Dei, causa secunda libera manet quoad potentiam & usum potentiae, ad agendum, vel non agendum, adeo ut actionem suam, si velit, suspendere possit. alteram talem, qua posita non manet libera causa secunda, saltem non ad usum potentiae, ut actionem suam suspendere possit, posita actione, motione, & impulsu Dei; sed ex qua fit ut necessario in alteram partem flectatur, ablata indifferentia ad alterutram partem; antequam actus ipse determinatus productus sit a creatura libera. Si priore modo vox determinationis intelligatur, talem determinationem Dei non negat respectu futurorum liberorum & contingentium. Sed si secundo sensu sumatur vox determinationis, plane negat Deum futura contingentia decreto suo determinasse ad alterutram partem.
latin.2098: II. Porro distincte non explicat quomodo ista simul constent, ut actio quaedam aeterno Dei decreto determinata sit, & tamen posita illa determinatione voluntas semper maneat indifferens ad talem actionem, & possit semper illam elicere, vel non elicere. Ex iis tamen quae subjungit colligendum relinquit rem ita se habere, quoniam Deus ut sua decreta circa hominum actus exequatur, non aliter movet eorum voluntatem quam iis administrando & proponendo ea objecta atque argumenta, quibus ad volendum quidem inducantur, sed ita tamen ut semper in eorum potestate sit objectis illis non moveri. Verum illius Discipuli, ut inter alios Nicolaus Grevinchovius, ad nodum hunc solvendum diserte adhibent scientiam mediam, sicuti solent Jesuitae plurimi, qua ratione thesibus praecedentibus expositum fuit.
latin.2099: III. Sed inter eos etiam Reformatos qui alioqui videntur ab Arminiano dogmate alieni, & Dordracenae Synodo subscribunt, reperiuntur nonnulli qui hanc quoque viam sequuntur, ut Providentiae Divinae decreta cum arbitrii humani libertate concilient. Quo de numero est Robertus Baronius Abredoniae in Scotia ante aliquot annos Theologiae Professor. Is enim in Metaphysica ad Theologiae usum accommodata Fonsecae doctrinam hac in parte laudat, eique aperte subscribit. Sect. 12. disput. 2. num. 65.
latin.2100: IV. Nam eo in loco proponit duas conclusiones Fonsecae quas dicit sibi maxime utiles videri ad stabiliendam concordiam Providentiae Divinae, & libertatis arbitrii humani. Prior est quod ante omnem praescientiam actuum liberorum eorum nullus fuit ab aeterno praedefinitus. Quorum verborum, inquit, hic sensus est, Antequam Deus praescivit, vel praevidit in quam partem humanae voluntates inclinaturae essent, si hae vel illae occasiones iis offerrentur, non absolute voluit voluntatem elicere has actiones potius quam illas, neque decrevit concurrere ad eliciendas has actiones potius quam illas. Secunda conclusio est, Postquam Deus secundum nostrum concipiendi modum praevidit in quam partem inclinaturae essent nostrae voluntates, cum hae aut illae occasiones iis offerrentur, ab aeterno decrevit cum voluntatibus nostris concurrere ad eliciendas, in hoc vel illo tempore, has vel illas actiones, in quas voluntates inclinaturas praevidebat. Exempli causa, Deus ab aeterno praevidit Adamum, si tentaretur ab Uxore, appetiturum pomum, & propterea decrevit concurrere cum Adamo ad eliciendam appetitionem pomi.
latin.2101: V. Sic ergo explicari posse putat ordinem Decreti Divini circa primum illud peccatum. Primo, inquit, Deus habet praescientiam conditionatam qua praevidet Adamum appetiturum pomum si offeratur illi talis occasio; habet item praescientiam, qua novit se posse illam actionem Adami dirigere ad gloriam suam. Secundo, quia praevidit se posse ex illa prava actione Adami, quam Adamus habiturus esset, si ei offeratur talis occasio; quia, inquam, praevidit se posse ex illa actione magnum bonum elicere, scilicet, manifestationem gloriae suae, ideo voluit illam occasionem Adamo offerri, id est, voluit permittere Evam a Serpente seductam Adamum tentare. Tertio, secundum praescientiam non conditionatam, sed absolutam praevidit voluntatem Adami inclinaturam esse ad appetitionem pomi, eo scilicet tempore quo Adamus tentandus esset. Quarto, partim ne praeriperet Adamo usum sui liberi Arbitrii, partim ut gloriam suam manifestaret, decrevit concurrere cum voluntate Adami ad eliciendam illam volitionem. Unde evidenter patet non ideo Adamum fuisse lapsurum, vel appetiturum pomum, quia Deus decrevit cum ejus voluntate concurrere ad eliciendam appetitionem; sed contra, ideo Deum decrevisse concurrere ad eliciendam illam actionem potius quam aliam, quia praevidit voluntatem ejus in talem partem inclinaturam fuisse, cum talis occasio illi offerretur.
latin.2102: VI. Ex quibus postea dicit manifeste sequi Deum per decreta Providentiae suae non imponere nobis necessitatem hoc vel illud volendi: ac praeterea Dei decreta non esse causas cur hoc vel illo tempore, hanc vel illam volitionem eliciamus; & per consequens ex infallibilitate decretorum divinorum non sequi omnes actiones nostras liberas evenire necessario necessitate causali: quia tantum ex illa infallibilitate decretorum sequitur actiones nostras liberas evenire necessario ea necessitate consequentiae, quae non est causalis vel motiva. Atque adeo decreta Providentiae Dei non magis tollent libertatem arbitrii nostri, & contingentiam nostrarum actionum, quam praescientia Dei: sicut enim res non ideo eventura est, quia praescita est, ita etiam nos non ideo acturi sumus, secundum has vel illas actiones, quia Deus decrevit nobiscum concurrere ad has vel illas actiones eliciendas: sed potius Deus decrevit concurrere ad tales actiones, quia praevidit nos ita acturos.
latin.2103: VII. Joannes Strangius Scotus vir ante paucos annos inter suos celeberrimus, hic singulari quadam ratione philosophatur. Nam aeterna Dei decreta circa omnes & singulos hominum actus versari concedit, sed non eodem modo. Primo enim quod attinet actus malos, ex ejus sententia, objiciuntur decretis divinis, non quod Deus illos fieri decreverit & praedefinierit, sed quia Deus decrevit permittere ut fiant, tum bonum ex illis elicere, eosque ad fines varios ordinare. Illam autem permissionem efficacem esse negat, id est, talem, ut ea posita, necessario sequatur quicquid fieri permittitur.
latin.2104: VIII. Quod spectat autem actus quibus natura sua malitia annexa non est, vult eos omnes dici posse a Deo decretos atque praedefinitos, sed rursus non omnes eadem ratione. Alios enim, juxta ipsum, Deus absolute decrevit, alios autem respective. Intelligit autem illa absolute a Deo decerni & praedefiniri, quae ante considerationem voluntatis nostrae decrevit, imo ad quae statuit voluntatem nostram praedeterminare. Respective vero, quae Deus decrevit fore secundum liberam nostram electionem, in iis in quibus liberam nobis optionem concedit, ita ut licitum sit hoc vel illud eligere.
latin.2105: IX. Priori modo censet Deum decrevisse & praedefiniisse omnes actus vere bonos, & qui per se ad aeternam hominis salutem conferunt, ad quos Deus ab aeterno constituit voluntatem nostram efficaciter praedeterminare, ut revera illam in tempore actu praedeterminat. Sed praeter bona hominum opera, existimat quoque multa alia esse ex eorum genere quibus malitia necessario non adhaeret, ad quae voluntas hominum in tempore a Deo praedeterminatur, & consequenter quae fuerunt ab aeterno a Deo absolute decreta atque praedefinita, ut exempli gratia, heroica Cyri gesta, & quae erga Josephum Pharao Rex Aegypti gessit, & infinita ejusdem generis.
latin.2106: X. Veruntamen ut putat voluntatem hominum ad multos actus etiam ex se non malos, absolute a Deo in tempore non praedeterminari, sed liberam ipsi optionem permitti, ex duobus aut pluribus, quae utraque aut omnia sunt licita; sic etiam non putat omnes voluntatis actus, etiam qui peccati rationem non habent, fuisse absolute a Deo praedefinitos in aeternis ipsius decretis: sed, ut loquitur, respective solum; quia scilicet, praedefiniti non sunt ante & citra considerationem determinationis voluntatis creatae, sed cum respectu ad eam.
latin.2107: XI. Verbi causa, inquit, tria ista quae Deus permisit Optioni Davidis capite vigesimo quarto libri secundi Samuelis, omnia erant licita, id est, quodvis eorum potuit David licite eligere. Permissio enim horum Dei respectu non solum fuit Physica, sed etiam moralis. Deus permisit ei liberam optionem, ut quodcunque ex tribus mallet, id eligeret, non restrinxit ad unum, itaque non decrevit ut solum unum eligeret: sed praescius futurae electionis Davidis, ejusque habita ratione, recte dici potest simpliciter decrevisse pestem futuram, & septuaginta millia hominum occisum iri. Deus enim decrevit id efficere quod David electurus erat, hoc autem electurum eum Deus praeviderat; ergo hoc idem efficere Deus decrevit. De voluntate Dei circa peccatum lib. 3. cap. 2.
latin.2108: XII. Ibidem vero rem illam illustrat simili quod occurrit inter homines. Si rex, inquit, servo suo optionem concedat hoc vel illud, vel tertium praemium aut munus eligendi ac petendi, certe non decrevit eum restringere ad unum horum; sed decrevit dare ei illud certum praemium, aut munus quod ille elegerit aut petierit. Multo magis id de Deo dici potest. Rex enim servo optionem dedit, ignarus forte ac incertus quid ille electurus esset. At Deo, quem nihil latere potest, ab aeterno certum erat quid David electurus esset.
latin.2109: XIII. Sub finem vero capitis rem eandem accuratius explicat his verbis, Quotiescunque Deus permittit creatae voluntatis arbitrio electionem & optionem ad duo aut plura, vel ad agendum aut non agendum, non est existimandum Deum illam ad unam duntaxat partem restringere. Sed si decreto permissionis praescientiam Dei conjungamus de eventu futuro, sic dici potest Deum praedefinivisse singulos actus licitos qui eveniunt, quia ipse eam libertatem voluntati concedit, & cum ea cooperatur, idemque ab aeterno decrevit. Non quod Deus prius praeviderit eventum futurum, ac deinde eum decreverit fore; id enim ineptum esset, nempe illud decernere futurum, quod ante decretum praescivit esse futurum; nec quod Deus prius absolute decernat, ac deinde id praesciat futurum. Nam sic non permisisset, nec decrevisset permittere libero voluntatis arbitrio ut id & aliud ageret & non ageret: sed quod uno eodemque instanti simul praesciat ac decernat seu praedefiniat. Certe in aeternitate nihil est prius aut posterius; itaque cum praescientia & praedefinitio sint ab aeterno, neutra est altera prior aut posterior. Nos quidem pro nostro concipiendi modo, diversa rationis instantia distinguimus in aeternis Dei actibus. Sed nec secundum instantia rationis unam altera priorem aut posteriorem dicimus.
latin.2110: XIV. Ut autem decreta divina cum voluntatis humanae libertate conciliet, duplicem voluntatis libertatem distinguit. Unam latius & communius sumptam, quae voluntati essentialis est, & in eo consistit quod voluntas proprio suo motu, certoque rationis judicio movetur: Alteram sensu strictiore acceptam, quam constituit in quadam voluntatis indifferentia ad opposita duo vel plura. Decreta Dei quibus absolute voluntatis actus praedefiniti sunt, fatetur hanc posteriorem libertatem tollere, quandoquidem voluntatem ad unum praedeterminant, nec sinunt amplius eam indifferentem ut agat vel non agat: sed ex ejus sententia voluntatem non privant libertate priori, quia haec optime consistunt, ut voluntas rationis judicium sequatur, & motu naturae suae consentaneo feratur, & tamen ad agendum a Deo praedefinita, & in tempore praedeterminata sit; quoniam scilicet, Deus voluntatem movet suaviter, & eo modo qui congruit & conveniens est naturae voluntatis.
latin.2111: XV. Caeterum decreta Dei quibus mala fieri permittit, aut quosdam voluntatis actus non absolute sed tantum respective praedefinivit, voluntatem, juxta ipsum, liberam sinunt non solum priori & latiori sensu, sed etiam sensu illo posteriori atque strictiori, quia nempe antecedenter ad voluntatis ipsius determinationem, ab ea non auferunt indifferentiam ut agat vel non agat. Si quidem Dei permissio in eo statu voluntatem relinquit, ut possit quod permittitur agere vel non agere: quae vero sunt a Deo respective decreta, non, ut jam dictum est, praedefinita sunt ante & citra considerationem determinationis ipsius voluntatis, quae prolixius exposita videre est apud eundem Strangium lib. 2. c. 8.
latin.2112: XVI. Proinde secundum hujus viri doctrinam, quanquam homo in pluribus quae in hac vita degens agit, illa libertate gaudeat quae sita est in potestate ad opposita se determinandi; plurium tamen aliorum respectu quae sunt absolute Dei decreto praedefinita, libertatem eam non retinet, sed eam solum quae in eo sita est quod homo libens agit, & ex rationis propriae judicio. Quod praecipue locum habere putat in conversione hominis ad Deum & operibus gratiae. Nam, inquit, citra praedeterminationem Dei non potest homo converti, non potest pie agere; & posita praedeterminatione gratiae, non potest non converti, non potest non pie agere. Proinde in illis operibus etsi agnoscamus manere libertatem, quae voluntati est essentialis, tamen libertatem in strictiore isto sensu usurpatam illic locum habere negamus.
latin.2113: XVII. Hic quoque viam singularem sequi videtur inclytae & celeberrimae memoriae vir Moses Amyraldus. Ille ergo quaecunque ab hominibus fiunt sive bona, sive mala, sive de eorum genere quae habentur indifferentia, aeternis Dei decretis designata, & praedefinita esse existimat, eaque decreta certissime & indeclinabiliter executioni mandari: sic tamen ut nec in eo violetur hominis libertas, nec Deus autor peccati statuatur.
latin.2114: XVIII. Ut autem modum explicet quo ista simul constant, supponit hominis facultates liberas, quales sunt juxta ipsum intellectus & voluntas, ab objectis determinari. Voluntatem enim necessario sequi dictamen intellectus, neque hominem posse aliter velle quam volendum esse judicat: Si vero intellectui sic vel sic affecto atque disposito, objectum hoc aut illud, sub tali luce proponatur, id est, his vel illis rationum momentis instructum & munitum, ita ut sit proportio & convenientia inter objectum tale & intellectum prout tunc se habet, necessario intellectum ad assensum vel dissensum determinandum esse, & hoc aut illud judicium de objecto sibi oblato determinate pronunciaturum, prout exiget ista proportio seu convenientia, quae inter intellectum & objectum fore supponitur.
latin.2115: XIX. Nec istam necessitatem seu determinationem, quae juxta ipsum oritur a convenientia objecti cum facultate, libertati quicquam officere putat, quoniam libertatem non constituit in facultatis liberae indeterminatione & indifferentia & immunitate ab omni necessitate, sed cum ea pugnare putat eam solum necessitatem quae est a vi externa, a materia, vel a sensu, quam Physicam & brutam appellare possumus, aut saltem eam quae tollit omnem consultationem & deliberationem.
latin.2116: XX. Deinde Providentiae Divinae efficaciam qua divina decreta executioni mandantur, respectu humanarum actionum in genere, in eo constituit quod Deus hominis facultates conservat, & objecta varia modis variis atque innumeris illis offerri vel auferri vel sinit vel procurat; Unde necessario & infallibiliter oriuntur actiones decretis Dei designatae, & tamen liberarum facultatum naturae ac dispositioni, & objectorum ipsis propositorum conditioni congruentes, ac proinde liberae: quandoquidem vis nulla facultatibus illata est, nec earum libertatem ullo modo violat objectorum quorumcunque oblatio & propositio.
latin.2117: XXI. Speciatim vero respectu bonarum actionum, praeterea quae jam dicta sunt, non aliud Deo tribuit quam quod facultates ipsas ab adnatis vitiis repurgat, aut novis viribus instruit, & supra nativam ac primigeniam conditionem elevat, quibus actionibus libertatem earum nihil omnino laedi sed adjuvari potius planum est.
latin.2118: XXII. Quod spectat autem malas actiones quantumcunque decretis divinis subjaceant, ex suis principiis ostendi facile posse existimat Deum nullatenus earum authorem dici posse: quoniam Deus hominum mentem & voluntatem ad malum non inclinat, nec eas ulla ratione vitiat, sed solum proprios motus ultro exerere sinit: neque alia ratione circa eas versatur divina providentia, quam quod ista potius quam alia objecta, hacque potius quam illa ratione ipsis offerri procurat aut permittit. Unde tamen necessario resultant istae vel illae actiones, prout exigit relatio proportionis & convenientiae inter talia objecta, & facultates sic vel sic affectas. Quo fit ut decreta divina de illis & circa illas indeclinabiliter executioni mandentur: nec minus interea facultates ipsae libere moveantur; quandoquidem vis nulla ipsis infertur, neque aliter agunt quam fert ipsarum natura atque dispositio.
latin.2119: XXIII. Cum ergo Deus circa hominum facultates, seu in bonum seu in malum ferantur, nihil operetur quod cum earum nativa libertate repugnet, & tamen ad Dei operationem infallibiliter sequantur isti vel illi actus sive boni sive mali; Deus autem non aliter res ab aeterno decreverit quam exequitur in tempore: inde colligit haec optime consistere, ut homines libere agant, & interim dum libere agunt ea peragant inevitabiliter quae aeternis Dei decretis constituta & designata sunt. Quae latius diducta videre licet apud virum illum Doctissimum disputatione de libero arbitrio capite quarto.
latin.2120: XXIV. Caeterum ad difficultatem istam expediendam viam paulo diversam insistunt Scholae Reformatae Theologi complures. Non solum enim docent quaecunque ab hominibus fiunt aeternis Dei decretis esse praedefinita, sed decreta illa putant effectum suum sortiri, non solum, ut censet vir ille Doctissimus, per aliquam facultatum liberarum immutationem, quae in earum restitutione, aut novarum virium adjectione consistat, ac praeterea per variorum objectorum tum intus tum extra propositionem, verum etiam per physicam & realem efficaciam, qua facultates ipsae ad hos & illos actus liberos praemoveantur, & praedeterminentur.
latin.2121: XXV. Nempe haec est eorum doctrina, Absoluto & energetico ut loquuntur Dei decreto quaecunque fiunt a causis etiam liberis & contingentibus decreta & ordinata esse. Hoc decretum nunquam irritum esse posse, sed omnino necesse esse ut impleantur quae sic a Deo decreta sunt. Adeoque illa ipsa quae causae contingentes & liberae operantur, hujus decreti respectu necessario fieri nec aliter evenire posse.

sections.title: Arminius and the Remonstrants side with Molina; Arminius's two senses of determination
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. James Arminius, and those who having followed his dogmas in the Low Countries are called Remonstrants, as in explaining the nature of human freedom they agree with Molina and his disciples; so also they seem to reconcile it in the same way with the decrees of Divine Providence. At least thither tend the things which Arminius teaches in the Response to Article 7, of his Works page 143. Where he does not indeed deny that God by his eternal Decree predefined and predetermined future contingents; but he distinguishes a double determination of God by which he establishes that something be done: One such, that, any action, motion, impulse of God whatever being posited, the free second cause remains free as to the power and the use of the power, for acting, or not acting, so that it can suspend its action, if it will. The other such, that being posited the second cause does not remain free, at least not for the use of the power, so that it can suspend its action, the action, motion and impulse of God being posited; but from which it comes about that it is necessarily bent to one part, the indifference to either part being taken away; before the determined act itself is produced by the free creature. If the word determination be understood in the former way, he does not deny such a determination of God with respect to future free and contingent things. But if the word determination be taken in the second sense, he plainly denies that God by his decree determined future contingents to either part.
pass_b: James Arminius, and those in the Low Countries who followed his teachings and are called Remonstrants, agree with Molina and his disciples in explaining the nature of human freedom. They also seem to reconcile that freedom with the decrees of God's providence in the same way. Arminius's teaching in his Response to Article 7, Works page 143, at least points that way.

There he does not deny that God by his eternal decree predefined and predetermined future contingents. But he distinguishes two kinds of divine determination by which God settles that something shall happen. In the first, whatever action, motion or impulse of God is in place, the free second cause remains free both in its power and in the use of that power to act or not act, so that it can suspend its action if it wishes.

In the second, once God's action, motion and impulse are in place, the second cause does not remain free, at least not in the use of its power so as to be able to suspend its action. Instead it is necessarily bent to one side, its indifference to either side being removed, before the determined act is produced by the free creature.

If 'determination' is taken in the first sense, he does not deny that God so determines future free and contingent things. If it is taken in the second sense, he flatly denies that God by his decree determined future contingents to one side or the other.

lemmas.gloss: they agree with Molina and his disciples
he distinguishes a double determination of God
the indifference to either part being taken away

choices.why: The Thomist term for God's determining the created will to its act beforehand; kept as 'predetermine', with 'premove' for praemovere.

notes: Jacobus Arminius (1560-1609), 'Apologia adversus articulos XXXI', art. 7, in Opera theologica (Leiden, 1629), p. 143.

sections.title: Arminius does not say how determination and indifference cohere; his disciples (Grevinchoven) use middle knowledge
sections.pass_a: II. Further he does not distinctly explain how these stand together, that some action be determined by God's eternal decree, and yet that determination being posited the will always remain indifferent to such an action, and be always able to elicit it, or not elicit it. Yet from the things which he subjoins he leaves it to be gathered that the matter is so, since God, that he may execute his decrees about the acts of men, does not otherwise move their will than by administering and proposing to them those objects and arguments, by which they are indeed induced to will, but yet so that it is always in their power not to be moved by those objects. But his Disciples, as among others Nicolaus Grevinchovius, expressly apply middle knowledge to untie this knot, as most Jesuits are accustomed, in the way which was set forth in the preceding theses.
pass_b: He does not clearly explain how these two things fit together: that an action is determined by God's eternal decree, and yet, with that determination in place, the will always remains indifferent to the action and always able to produce it or not.

From what he adds, however, he leaves us to infer that it works like this. To carry out his decrees about human acts, God moves men's wills only by supplying and setting before them objects and arguments that do induce them to will, yet in such a way that it always remains in their power not to be moved by those objects.
His disciples, such as Nicolaus Grevinchoven among others, expressly bring in middle knowledge to untie this knot, as most Jesuits do, in the way set out in the preceding theses.

lemmas.latin: distincte non explicat quomodo ista simul constent

notes: Nicolaus Grevinchovius (Grevinchoven, d. 1632), Remonstrant minister of Rotterdam.

sections.title: Some Reformed who subscribe Dort take the same way, notably Robert Baron of Aberdeen, who follows Fonseca
sections.pass_a: III. But among those Reformed also who otherwise seem alien from the Arminian dogma, and subscribe the Synod of Dort, some are found who also follow this way, that they may reconcile the decrees of Divine Providence with the freedom of human choice. Of which number is Robert Baron, some years ago Professor of Theology at Aberdeen in Scotland. For he in the Metaphysics accommodated to the use of Theology praises the doctrine of Fonseca in this part, and openly subscribes to it. Sect. 12. disput. 2. num. 65.
pass_b: Yet even among the Reformed who otherwise seem far from the Arminian teaching and subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some follow this same way of reconciling the decrees of God's providence with the freedom of human choice.

One of them is Robert Baron, some years ago professor of theology at Aberdeen in Scotland. In his Metaphysics adapted to the use of theology he praises Fonseca's teaching on this point and openly endorses it: section 12, disputation 2, number 65.

notes: Robert Baron (c. 1596-1639), professor of divinity at Marischal College, Aberdeen; Metaphysica generalis (published posthumously), sect. 12, disp. 2, n. 65. On Fonseca see De Decretis Pars Secunda XXXI.

sections.title: Baron cites Fonseca's two conclusions: nothing predefined before foreknowledge; concurrence decreed after it (Adam)
sections.pass_a: IV. For in that place he proposes two conclusions of Fonseca which he says seem to him most useful for establishing the concord of Divine Providence and of the freedom of human choice. The former is that before all foreknowledge of free acts none of them was predefined from eternity. Of which words, he says, this is the sense, Before God foreknew, or foresaw to which part human wills would incline, if these or those occasions were offered them, he did not absolutely will the will to elicit these actions rather than those, nor did he decree to concur to eliciting these actions rather than those. The second conclusion is, After God according to our mode of conceiving foresaw to which part our wills would incline, when these or those occasions were offered them, he decreed from eternity to concur with our wills to elicit, at this or that time, these or those actions, to which he foresaw the wills would incline. For example, God from eternity foresaw that Adam, if he were tempted by his Wife, would desire the apple, and therefore decreed to concur with Adam to eliciting the desire of the apple.
pass_b: Baron there cites two conclusions of Fonseca which, by his own account, strike him as especially helpful for showing that God's providence and the freedom of human choice agree. First: none of our free acts was predefined from eternity prior to every foreknowledge of them.

He glosses this as follows. Until God had foreknown or foreseen in which direction human wills would turn, were this or that occasion put to them, he neither willed absolutely that the will should elicit one set of actions over another, nor decreed to concur in eliciting one set rather than another.

Second: once God, as we must conceive it, had foreseen the direction our wills would take when given this or that occasion, he decreed from eternity to concur with them at the relevant times in eliciting precisely the actions he saw they would turn toward.
Thus, to take an example, God foresaw from eternity that Adam, if tempted by his wife, would desire the fruit, and for that reason decreed to concur with Adam in eliciting that desire.

sections.title: Baron's four steps in God's decree about the first sin
sections.pass_a: V. Thus therefore he thinks the order of the Divine Decree about that first sin can be explained. First, he says, God has conditional foreknowledge by which he foresees that Adam will desire the apple if such an occasion be offered him; he has likewise a foreknowledge, by which he knew he could direct that action of Adam to his glory. Second, because he foresaw that he could from that depraved action of Adam, which Adam would have, if such an occasion were offered him; because, I say, he foresaw he could elicit from that action a great good, namely, the manifestation of his glory, therefore he willed that occasion to be offered to Adam, that is, he willed to permit Eve seduced by the Serpent to tempt Adam. Third, according to foreknowledge not conditional, but absolute he foresaw that the will of Adam would incline to the desire of the apple, namely at that time when Adam was to be tempted. Fourth, partly lest he should snatch from Adam the use of his free Choice, partly that he might manifest his glory, he decreed to concur with the will of Adam to elicit that volition. Whence it evidently appears that Adam was not therefore about to fall, or to desire the apple, because God decreed to concur with his will to elicit the desire; but on the contrary, that God therefore decreed to concur to elicit that action rather than another, because he foresaw that his will would incline to such a part, when such an occasion was offered him.
pass_b: So he thinks the order of God's decree about that first sin can be explained as follows. 'First,' he says, 'God has a conditional foreknowledge by which he foresees that Adam will desire the fruit if such an occasion is offered him. He also has a foreknowledge by which he knew that he could direct that act of Adam to his own glory.

Second, he foresaw that from the wicked act Adam would perform if such an occasion were offered him, he could bring a great good, namely the display of his glory. Because of this, I say, he willed that the occasion be offered to Adam; that is, he willed to permit Eve, deceived by the serpent, to tempt Adam.
Third, by a foreknowledge that is not conditional but absolute, he foresaw that Adam's will would lean toward desiring the fruit at the time when Adam was to be tempted.
Fourth, partly so as not to take from Adam the use of his free choice, and partly to display his glory, he decreed to concur with Adam's will in producing that volition.

From this it plainly follows that Adam was not going to fall, or to desire the fruit, because God decreed to concur with his will in producing the desire. On the contrary, God decreed to concur in producing that action rather than another because he foresaw that Adam's will would lean that way when such an occasion was offered him.'

sections.title: Hence, says Baron, the decrees impose no causal necessity, only necessity of consequence, no more than foreknowledge
sections.pass_a: VI. From which things he afterwards says it manifestly follows that God through the decrees of his Providence does not impose on us a necessity of willing this or that: and moreover that the decrees of God are not causes why at this or that time we elicit this or that volition; and consequently from the infallibility of the divine decrees it does not follow that all our free actions come about necessarily by causal necessity: because from that infallibility of the decrees it only follows that our free actions come about necessarily by that necessity of consequence, which is not causal or motive. And so the decrees of God's Providence will not take away the freedom of our choice, and the contingency of our actions, more than God's foreknowledge: for as a thing is not therefore going to happen, because it is foreknown, so also we are not therefore going to act, according to these or those actions, because God decreed to concur with us to eliciting these or those actions: but rather God decreed to concur to such actions, because he foresaw we would so act.
pass_b: From this, he goes on to say, it plainly follows that God by the decrees of his providence does not impose on us a necessity of willing this or that. Nor are God's decrees the causes why we produce this or that volition at this or that time.

So it does not follow from the infallibility of the divine decrees that all our free actions come about necessarily by a causal necessity. From that infallibility it follows only that our free actions come about necessarily by the necessity of consequence, which is neither causal nor motive.

Thus the decrees of God's providence will no more remove the freedom of our choice and the contingency of our actions than God's foreknowledge does. A thing will not come about because it is foreknown; likewise we shall not act in these or those ways because God decreed to concur with us in producing these or those actions. Rather, God decreed to concur in such actions because he foresaw that we would act so.

sections.title: John Strang: decrees cover all acts, but not in the same way; evil acts are objects of a non-efficacious permission
sections.pass_a: VII. John Strang the Scot, a man a few years ago most celebrated among his own, philosophizes here in a certain singular way. For he concedes that the eternal decrees of God are concerned with all and single acts of men, but not in the same way. For first as regards evil acts, in his opinion, they are objects of the divine decrees, not because God decreed and predefined them to be done, but because God decreed to permit that they be done, then to elicit good from them, and to order them to various ends. But he denies that permission to be efficacious, that is, such, that it being posited, whatever is permitted to be done necessarily follows.
pass_b: The Scot John Strang, a few years ago one of the most celebrated men of his own side, reasons here in a way of his own. He grants that God's eternal decrees concern each and every human act, but not all in the same way.

First, evil acts, in his view, are objects of the divine decrees not because God decreed and predefined that they should be done, but because God decreed to permit them to be done, then to bring good out of them and order them to various ends. He denies, however, that this permission is efficacious, that is, such that once it is in place whatever is permitted follows necessarily.

sections.title: Strang: acts not evil in themselves are all decreed, some absolutely, some respectively
sections.pass_a: VIII. But as regards acts to which malice is not annexed by their nature, he wills that they all can be said to be decreed and predefined by God, but again not all in the same way. For some, according to him, God decreed absolutely, but others respectively. He understands those to be decreed and predefined by God absolutely, which he decreed before the consideration of our will, nay to which he determined to predetermine our will. But respectively, those which God decreed to be according to our free election, in those in which he grants us free option, so that it is lawful to choose this or that.
pass_b: As for acts that are not by their nature joined to malice, he holds that all of them can be said to be decreed and predefined by God, but again not all in the same way. Some, on his view, God decreed absolutely, others respectively.

By 'absolutely' decreed and predefined he means those that God decreed before considering our will, indeed those to which he resolved to predetermine our will. By 'respectively' he means those that God decreed would come about according to our free choice, in matters where he grants us a free option, so that we may lawfully choose this or that.

sections.title: In the first way God decreed all truly good acts and many indifferent ones (Cyrus, Pharaoh and Joseph)
sections.pass_a: IX. In the former way he judges that God decreed and predefined all truly good acts, and which of themselves conduce to the eternal salvation of man, to which God from eternity determined efficaciously to predetermine our will, as in fact he predetermines it in act in time. But besides the good works of men, he thinks also that there are many others of that kind to which malice does not necessarily adhere, to which the will of men is predetermined by God in time, and consequently which were from eternity absolutely decreed and predefined by God, as for example, the heroic deeds of Cyrus, and what Pharaoh King of Egypt did toward Joseph, and infinite things of the same kind.
pass_b: In the first way, he judges, God decreed and predefined all truly good acts, those that of themselves contribute to man's eternal salvation. To these God resolved from eternity to predetermine our will efficaciously, just as in time he actually does predetermine it.

Besides men's good works, he also thinks there are many other acts of a kind to which malice does not necessarily cling, to which God predetermines men's wills in time. These were therefore decreed and predefined by God absolutely from eternity: for example, the heroic deeds of Cyrus, what Pharaoh king of Egypt did for Joseph, and countless things of the same kind.

sections.title: Yet many acts not evil are left to free option, and are predefined only respectively, with regard to the will's determination
sections.pass_a: X. Nevertheless as he thinks the will of men to many acts even not evil of themselves, is not absolutely predetermined by God in time, but free option is permitted to it, out of two or more, which both or all are lawful; so also he does not think that all acts of the will, even those which have not the nature of sin, were absolutely predefined by God in his eternal decrees: but, as he speaks, respectively only; because namely, they were not predefined before and apart from the consideration of the determination of the created will, but with respect to it.
pass_b: Even so, he thinks that for many acts which are not evil in themselves, men's wills are not absolutely predetermined by God in time; they are left a free option between two or more alternatives, all of them lawful.

Likewise he does not think that all acts of the will, even those without the character of sin, were absolutely predefined by God in his eternal decrees. They were predefined, in his phrase, only 'respectively': not before and apart from considering how the created will would determine itself, but with regard to that determination.

sections.title: Strang's example: David's three options (2 Samuel 24); God decreed what David would choose
sections.pass_a: XI. For example, he says, those three things which God permitted to David's Option in the twenty-fourth chapter of the second book of Samuel, were all lawful, that is, David could lawfully choose any one of them. For the permission of these on God's part was not only Physical, but also moral. God permitted him free option, that whichever of the three he preferred, he should choose it, he did not restrict him to one, and so did not decree that he should choose only one: but foreknowing David's future election, and having regard to it, he can rightly be said simply to have decreed that the plague would be, and that seventy thousand men would be slain. For God decreed to effect that which David was going to choose, and God had foreseen that he would choose this; therefore God decreed to effect this same thing. On the will of God concerning sin book 3, chap. 2.
pass_b: He offers an example, saying: the three things God left to David's choice in 2 Samuel 24 were all lawful options; David could rightly pick any of them, since God's leave here was moral and not merely physical.

God left him free to take whichever of the three he liked best, did not confine him to one, and so made no decree that he should choose only one. Yet because God knew in advance what David would choose and took that into account, one may rightly say that God simply decreed that pestilence should come and that seventy thousand men should be killed.

God decreed to carry out whatever David would choose; he had foreseen that David would choose this; so it was this that God decreed to carry out. (Strang, On the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 2.)

sections.title: His simile: a king who lets a servant choose a reward decrees to give whatever he chooses
sections.pass_a: XII. And in the same place he illustrates that matter by a simile which occurs among men. If a king, he says, grant his servant the option of choosing and asking this or that, or a third reward or gift, surely he did not decree to restrict him to one of these; but decreed to give him that certain reward, or gift which he shall have chosen or asked. Much more can this be said of God. For the king gave the servant the option, ignorant perhaps and uncertain what he would choose. But to God, from whom nothing can be hidden, it was certain from eternity what David would choose.
pass_b: In the same place he illustrates the point with a comparison from human life. 'If a king,' he says, 'gives his servant the option of choosing and asking for this reward or gift, or that one, or a third, he certainly has not decreed to restrict him to one of them. He has decreed to give him the particular reward or gift that the servant chooses or asks for.

This can be said of God much more. The king gave the servant the option perhaps without knowing, and uncertain, what he would choose. But to God, from whom nothing can be hidden, it was certain from eternity what David would choose.'

sections.title: Strang: with the decree of permission joined to foreknowledge, God predefined each lawful act, foreknowing and decreeing in one instant
sections.pass_a: XIII. But toward the end of the chapter he explains the same matter more accurately in these words, Whenever God permits to the choice of the created will the election and option between two or more, or to acting or not acting, it is not to be thought that God restricts it to one part only. But if we join to the decree of permission God's foreknowledge of the future event, it can thus be said that God predefined the single lawful acts which come about, because he himself grants that freedom to the will, and cooperates with it, and decreed the same from eternity. Not that God first foresaw the future event, and then decreed it to be; for that would be absurd, namely to decree that to be future, which before the decree he foreknew to be future; nor that God first absolutely decrees, and then foreknows it future. For thus he would not have permitted, nor would have decreed to permit to the free choice of the will to do and not do this and something else: but that in one and the same instant he at once foreknows and decrees or predefines. Certainly in eternity nothing is prior or posterior; and so since foreknowledge and predefinition are from eternity, neither is prior or posterior to the other. We indeed according to our mode of conceiving distinguish diverse instants of reason in the eternal acts of God. But not even according to instants of reason do we call one prior or posterior to the other.
pass_b: Toward the end of the chapter he explains the matter more precisely in these words. 'Whenever God leaves to the choice of the created will an election and option between two or more things, or between acting and not acting, we must not think that God restricts it to one side only.

But if we join to the decree of permission God's foreknowledge of the future event, it can be said that God predefined each lawful act that comes about. For he himself grants that freedom to the will, cooperates with it, and decreed the same from eternity.

This is not because God first foresaw the future event and then decreed that it would be; that would be absurd, to decree as future what he already foreknew to be future before the decree. Nor is it because God first decrees absolutely and then foreknows the thing as future. In that case he would not have permitted, or decreed to permit, the will's free choice to do and not do this and other things. It is because in one and the same instant he both foreknows and decrees, or predefines.

In eternity there is certainly nothing prior or posterior. Since foreknowledge and predefinition are both from eternity, neither comes before or after the other. In our way of conceiving we do distinguish different instants of reason in God's eternal acts. But even by instants of reason we do not call one of these prior or posterior to the other.'

sections.title: Strang's two freedoms: the essential freedom of spontaneous rational motion survives absolute decrees; indifference does not
sections.pass_a: XIV. But that he may reconcile the divine decrees with the freedom of the human will, he distinguishes a double freedom of the will. One taken more widely and commonly, which is essential to the will, and consists in this that the will is moved by its own proper motion, and a certain judgement of reason: The other taken in a stricter sense, which he places in a certain indifference of the will to two or more opposites. The decrees of God by which acts of the will are absolutely predefined, he confesses take away this latter freedom, since they predetermine the will to one, nor allow it any longer to be indifferent to act or not act: but in his opinion they do not deprive the will of the former freedom, because these stand together very well, that the will follow the judgement of reason, and be borne by a motion agreeable to its nature, and yet be predefined to act by God, and predetermined in time; since namely, God moves the will sweetly, and in that way which is congruous and suitable to the nature of the will.
pass_b: To reconcile the divine decrees with the freedom of the human will, he distinguishes two kinds of freedom of the will. One, taken more broadly and commonly, is essential to the will: it consists in the will's being moved by its own motion and by a definite judgement of reason. The other, taken in a stricter sense, he locates in a kind of indifference of the will toward two or more opposites.

He admits that the decrees of God by which acts of the will are absolutely predefined remove this second freedom, since they predetermine the will to one thing and no longer leave it indifferent to act or not act.

But on his view they do not deprive the will of the first freedom. It fits perfectly well that the will should follow the judgement of reason and be carried by a motion in keeping with its nature, and yet be predefined by God to act and predetermined in time. For God moves the will gently, in a way that suits and befits the will's nature.

sections.title: Decrees of permission and respective decrees leave the will free in both senses
sections.pass_a: XV. But the decrees of God by which he permits evils to be done, or predefined certain acts of the will not absolutely but only respectively, leave the will, according to him, free not only in the former and wider sense, but also in that latter and stricter sense, because namely antecedently to the determination of the will itself, they do not take from it the indifference to act or not act. Since indeed God's permission leaves the will in that state, that it can do or not do what is permitted: but those things which are decreed by God respectively, are not, as has already been said, predefined before and apart from the consideration of the determination of the will itself, which may be seen set forth more at length in the same Strang book 2. c. 8.
pass_b: The decrees of God by which he permits evils to be done, or by which he predefined certain acts of the will not absolutely but only respectively, leave the will free, on his view, not only in the first and broader sense but also in the second and stricter one. Prior to the will's own determination they do not take from it the indifference to act or not act.

God's permission leaves the will in a state where it can do or not do what is permitted. And what God decreed respectively was not, as already said, predefined before and apart from considering how the will itself would determine itself. This is set out at greater length in Strang, book 2, chapter 8.

sections.title: So for Strang, in conversion and works of grace man keeps only essential freedom, not indifference
sections.pass_a: XVI. Therefore according to the doctrine of this man, although man in most things which he does living in this life, enjoys that freedom which is placed in the power of determining himself to opposites; yet in respect of many others which are absolutely predefined by God's decree, he does not retain that freedom, but that only which is placed in this that man acts willingly, and from the judgement of his own reason. Which he thinks has place especially in the conversion of man to God and in works of grace. For, he says, without the predetermination of God man cannot be converted, cannot act piously; and the predetermination of grace being posited, he cannot not be converted, cannot not act piously. Therefore in those works although we acknowledge that the freedom remains, which is essential to the will, yet we deny that freedom used in that stricter sense has place there.
pass_b: On this man's teaching, then, in most of what he does in this life man enjoys the freedom that consists in the power to determine himself to either of two opposites. But with respect to many other acts that are absolutely predefined by God's decree he does not keep that freedom, only the freedom that consists in acting willingly and by the judgement of his own reason.

He thinks this holds above all in man's conversion to God and in the works of grace. 'Without God's predetermination,' he says, 'a man cannot be converted and cannot act piously; and once the predetermination of grace is in place, he cannot fail to be converted and cannot fail to act piously. So although we acknowledge that the freedom essential to the will remains in those works, we deny that freedom in the stricter sense has any place there.'

sections.title: Amyraut: the free faculties are determined by objects; the will follows the intellect, the intellect the object as proportioned
sections.pass_a: XVIII. But that he may explain the mode in which these stand together, he supposes that the free faculties of man, such as according to him are the intellect and the will, are determined by objects. For he judges that the will necessarily follows the dictate of the intellect, and that man cannot will otherwise than he judges is to be willed: But if to an intellect affected and disposed thus or thus, this or that object be proposed in such a light, that is, furnished and fortified with these or those weights of reasons, so that there is a proportion and fitness between such an object and the intellect as it then is, the intellect must necessarily be determined to assent or dissent, and will pronounce determinately this or that judgement about the object offered to it, as that proportion or fitness shall require, which is supposed to be between the intellect and the object.
pass_b: To explain how these things fit together, he assumes that man's free faculties, which on his view are the intellect and the will, are determined by their objects. He holds that the will necessarily follows the dictate of the intellect, and that a man cannot will otherwise than he judges ought to be willed.

Suppose an intellect affected and disposed in this or that way, and suppose this or that object is put before it in a certain light, that is, equipped and backed by these or those weighty reasons, so that there is a proportion and fit between such an object and the intellect as it then stands. Then the intellect must necessarily be determined to assent or dissent.
It must then pronounce this or that definite judgement about the object offered to it, as required by the proportion or fit assumed to hold between the intellect and the object.

Nor does he think that this necessity or determination, which according to him arises from the fitness of the object with the faculty, hinders freedom in any way, since he does not place freedom in the indetermination and indifference and immunity from all necessity of the free faculty, but thinks that only that necessity conflicts with it which is from external force, from matter, or from sense, which we may call Physical and brute, or at least that which takes away all consultation and deliberation.
pass_b: Nor does he think that this necessity or determination, which on his view arises from the fit between object and faculty, hinders freedom at all, since he does not place freedom in the free faculty's indetermination, indifference and immunity from all necessity.

He thinks freedom conflicts only with the necessity that comes from external force, from matter or from sense, which we may call physical and brute necessity, or at least with the necessity that removes all consultation and deliberation.

sections.title: Amyraut: providence executes the decrees by conserving the faculties and arranging the objects offered
sections.pass_a: XX. Then he places the efficacy of Divine Providence by which the divine decrees are put into execution, in respect of human actions in general, in this that God conserves the faculties of man, and either allows or procures that various objects be offered to them or taken away in various and innumerable ways; Whence necessarily and infallibly arise the actions designated by God's decrees, and yet congruous to the nature and disposition of the free faculties, and to the condition of the objects proposed to them, and therefore free: since no force is brought upon the faculties, nor does the offering and proposal of any objects whatever in any way violate their freedom.
pass_b: Next, with respect to human actions in general, he locates the efficacy of God's providence, by which the divine decrees are carried out, in this: God preserves man's faculties and, in various and countless ways, either allows or arranges that various objects be offered to them or withdrawn.

From this the actions designated by God's decrees arise necessarily and infallibly. Yet they suit the nature and disposition of the free faculties and the condition of the objects put before them, and so they are free. No force is brought to bear on the faculties, and the offering and presenting of objects of any kind in no way violates their freedom.

sections.title: For good actions Amyraut adds only the cleansing, strengthening and raising of the faculties
sections.pass_a: XXI. But specially in respect of good actions, besides what has already been said, he attributes nothing else to God than that he purges the faculties themselves from inborn vices, or furnishes them with new strength, and raises them above their native and original condition, by which actions it is plain their freedom is not hurt at all but rather helped.
pass_b: With respect to good actions in particular, beyond what has already been said, he ascribes to God only this: that he cleanses the faculties themselves of their inborn faults, or supplies them with new strength and raises them above their native, original condition.
Plainly such acts do not harm the faculties' freedom at all, but rather help it.

sections.title: For evil actions God neither inclines nor corrupts, but arranges objects; the result follows necessarily yet freely
sections.pass_a: XXII. But as regards evil actions however much they are subject to the divine decrees, he thinks it can easily be shown from his principles that God can in no way be called their author: since God does not incline the mind and will of men to evil, nor corrupts them in any way, but only allows them to put forth their own motions of their own accord: nor is divine providence concerned about them in any other way, than that it procures or permits these objects rather than others, and in this rather than that way, to be offered to them. Whence however these or those actions necessarily result, as the relation of proportion and fitness between such objects, and faculties so or so affected requires. Whence it comes that the divine decrees concerning them and about them are put into execution unswervingly: and none the less meanwhile the faculties themselves are moved freely; since no force is brought upon them, nor do they act otherwise than their nature and disposition bears.
pass_b: As for evil actions, however fully they are subject to the divine decrees, he thinks it can easily be shown from his principles that God can in no way be called their author. God does not incline men's minds and wills to evil or corrupt them in any way; he only allows them to put forth their own motions of their own accord.

Divine providence is involved with these actions only in arranging or permitting that these objects rather than others be offered to them, and in this way rather than that. From this, nevertheless, these or those actions necessarily result, as the relation of proportion and fit between such objects and faculties disposed in this or that way requires.

So the divine decrees about them are carried out without fail, and meanwhile the faculties themselves move freely, since no force is applied to them and they act only as their own nature and disposition lead.

sections.title: Amyraut's conclusion: men act freely and yet inevitably accomplish what the decrees appointed
sections.pass_a: XXIII. Since therefore God, concerning the faculties of men, whether they are borne to good or to evil, works nothing which conflicts with their native freedom, and yet upon God's operation these or those acts whether good or evil infallibly follow; and God decreed things from eternity not otherwise than he executes them in time: thence he gathers that these stand together very well, that men act freely, and meanwhile while they act freely they inevitably accomplish the things which have been constituted and designated by God's eternal decrees. Which may be seen drawn out more widely in that most Learned man in the disputation on free choice chapter four.
pass_b: God, then, does nothing to men's faculties, whether they are carried toward good or toward evil, that conflicts with their native freedom. Yet upon God's working these or those acts, good or evil, follow infallibly, and God decreed things from eternity exactly as he carries them out in time.

From this Amyraut concludes that it fits perfectly well that men act freely and that, while acting freely, they inevitably accomplish what God's eternal decrees have appointed and designated. This is worked out more fully by that most learned man in his disputation on free choice, chapter 4.

sections.title: Many Reformed add physical and real premotion and predetermination of the faculties
sections.pass_a: XXIV. But to dispatch that difficulty several Theologians of the Reformed School tread a somewhat different way. For they not only teach that whatever things are done by men are predefined by the eternal decrees of God, but think that those decrees obtain their effect, not only, as that most Learned man judges, through some change of the free faculties, which consists in their restoration, or the addition of new strength, and besides through the proposal of various objects both within and without, but also through a physical and real efficacy, by which the faculties themselves are premoved and predetermined to these and those free acts.
pass_b: To deal with this difficulty, however, a good number of theologians of the Reformed school take a somewhat different path. They teach not only that whatever men do is predefined by God's eternal decrees, but also that those decrees take effect by more than that most learned man holds.

They do not work only through some change in the free faculties, consisting in their restoration or the addition of new strength, together with the presenting of various objects from within and from without. They also work through a physical and real efficacy by which the faculties themselves are premoved and predetermined to these and those free acts.

choices.why: The Thomist term for God's determining the created will to its act beforehand; kept as 'predetermine', with 'premove' for praemovere.

sections.title: Their teaching: all events, even free and contingent ones, are decreed by an absolute, energetic decree that cannot fail
sections.pass_a: XXV. Namely this is their doctrine, That by an Absolute and energetic decree of God, as they speak, whatever things are done by causes even free and contingent, have been decreed and ordered. That this decree can never be void, but that it is altogether necessary that the things so decreed by God be fulfilled. And so that those very things which contingent and free causes work, are necessarily done in respect of this decree, nor can come out otherwise.
pass_b: Their teaching is this. By an absolute and, as they call it, 'energetic' decree of God, whatever is done even by free and contingent causes has been decreed and ordered. This decree can never fail, and what God has so decreed must without exception be fulfilled.
So the very things that contingent and free causes do are done necessarily with respect to this decree, and cannot turn out otherwise.

lemmas.latin: Absoluto & energetico ut loquuntur Dei decreto
lemmas.gloss: by an Absolute and energetic decree of God, as they speak

lemmas.latin: Hoc decretum nunquam irritum esse posse
